subject: General Physiology
front: What percentage of body weight is Total Body Water (TBW)?
back: 60% of body weight is water

subject: General Physiology
front: How does TBW compare between males and females?
back: TBW is greater in males than in females

subject: General Physiology
front: How does TBW change with age?
back: TBW decreases with age

subject: General Physiology
front: Which substances/markers are used to measure total body water?
back: D2O (deuterium oxide), T2O (tritiated water), and Antipyrine

subject: General Physiology
front: What fraction of TBW is intracellular fluid (ICF)?
back: 2/3 of total body water

subject: General Physiology
front: What fraction of TBW is extracellular fluid (ECF)?
back: 1/3 of total body water

subject: General Physiology
front: Why can't ICF volume be measured directly?
back: Because it is inside the cells, so it cannot be measured directly; it is calculated as TBW minus ECF

subject: General Physiology
front: Which substances are used to measure ECF volume?
back: Mannitol, sucrose, inulin, and sodium thiosulfate (substances that do not enter cells)

subject: General Physiology
front: ECF is further divided into which two compartments?
back: Interstitial fluid and plasma

subject: General Physiology
front: What fraction of ECF is interstitial fluid?
back: 3/4 of ECF (the major portion)

subject: General Physiology
front: What fraction of ECF is plasma?
back: 1/4 of ECF (the minor portion)

subject: General Physiology
front: Can interstitial fluid volume be measured directly?
back: No, it cannot be measured directly; it is calculated as ECF minus plasma volume

subject: General Physiology
front: Which substances are used to measure plasma volume?
back: RISA (Radio-Iodinated Serum Albumin) and Evans blue (T-1824)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is transcellular fluid and what are examples?
back: Fluid separated from plasma by an extra layer of epithelium; examples include synovial fluid and pleural fluid

subject: General Physiology
front: A patient is injected with 500 mg mannitol. Plasma mannitol concentration is 3 mg/dL, and 10% of the dose is excreted in urine before equilibrium. What volume/compartment is being estimated, and what is its value?
back: The extracellular fluid volume is estimated. Volume = mass/concentration = (500 - 10% of 500)/3 = 450/3 = 150 dL = 15 L

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the major cations of ECF?
back: Sodium (Na+) and Calcium (Ca2+)

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the major cations of ICF?
back: Potassium (K+) and Magnesium (Mg2+)

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the major anions of ECF?
back: Chloride (Cl-) and Bicarbonate (HCO3-)

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the major anions of ICF?
back: Phosphate and proteins

subject: General Physiology
front: How does protein content compare between ECF and ICF?
back: ECF has low protein content while ICF has high protein content

subject: General Physiology
front: How does pH compare between ECF and ICF?
back: ECF pH is higher/more alkaline (~7.4), while ICF pH is lower/more acidic (~7.0)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the major buffer of ECF?
back: Bicarbonate (HCO3-)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the major buffer of ICF?
back: Proteins

subject: General Physiology
front: Approximately what are plasma vs ICF sodium concentrations?
back: Plasma (ECF) Na+ is about 142 mEq/L, while ICF Na+ is about 10 mEq/L

subject: General Physiology
front: Approximately what are plasma vs ICF potassium concentrations?
back: Plasma (ECF) K+ is about 4 mEq/L, while ICF K+ is about 140 mEq/L

subject: General Physiology
front: Approximately what are ECF vs ICF protein concentrations?
back: ECF protein is about 2 g/dL (5 mEq/L), while ICF protein is about 16 g/dL (40 mEq/L)

subject: General Physiology
front: In a Darrow-Yannet diagram, what are the two axes and two compartments plotted?
back: Volume is plotted on the x-axis and osmolality on the y-axis, showing ICF and ECF as adjacent boxes

subject: General Physiology
front: Which compartment is initially affected by any fluid loss or gain?
back: The ECF compartment is initially affected

subject: General Physiology
front: Why must ICF and ECF eventually reach the same osmolality after a fluid shift?
back: Because free water moves from the more dilute compartment to the less dilute compartment (like osmosis) until osmolalities equalize

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the first step when approaching a Darrow-Yannet diagram problem?
back: Determine whether the ECF volume is contracted (fluid loss) or expanded (fluid gain)

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the fluid shift, osmolality change, and give examples for isotonic fluid loss.
back: Only ECF volume decreases; overall osmolality is unchanged (no free water shift); examples: hemorrhage, diarrhea (the older Cerebellum PDF also lists vomiting as an example)

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the fluid shift, osmolality change, and give examples for hypertonic fluid loss.
back: ECF osmolality is reduced, so ECF gives free water to ICF (ICF expands, ECF shrinks further); overall osmolality is reduced; examples: Addison's disease, loop diuretics

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the fluid shift, osmolality change, and give examples for hypotonic fluid loss.
back: ECF osmolality increases, so ICF gives free water to ECF (ICF shrinks further); overall osmolality increases; examples: sweating (water loss > Na+ loss), diabetes insipidus

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the fluid shift, osmolality change, and give an example for isotonic fluid gain.
back: Only ECF volume increases; overall osmolality is unchanged; example: crystalloid infusion

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the fluid shift, osmolality change, and give an example for hypertonic fluid gain.
back: ECF osmolality increases, so ICF gives free water to ECF (ICF shrinks, ECF expands more); overall osmolality increases; example: 3% NaCl infusion

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the fluid shift, osmolality change, and give examples for hypotonic fluid gain.
back: ECF osmolality decreases, so ECF gives free water to ICF (ICF expands, ECF expands less); overall osmolality is reduced; examples: polydipsia, SIADH

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the resting membrane potential (RMP) of a nerve cell?
back: -70 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: What ion movement maintains the RMP?
back: K+ leaking out of the cell (K+ efflux via leaky channels)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is primarily responsible for maintaining RMP?
back: The high resting permeability of the membrane to K+

subject: General Physiology
front: What ion movement causes depolarization?
back: Na+ influx into the cell

subject: General Physiology
front: What channel event underlies depolarization?
back: Opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels

subject: General Physiology
front: What ion movement causes repolarization?
back: K+ efflux out of the cell

subject: General Physiology
front: What two channel changes occur together during repolarization?
back: K+ channels open (causing efflux) while Na+ channels inactivate

subject: General Physiology
front: What ion movement causes hyperpolarization?
back: Continued K+ efflux beyond the resting potential

subject: General Physiology
front: Why does hyperpolarization make the membrane more negative than RMP?
back: Because K+ efflux continues even after the membrane reaches RMP

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the threshold (trigger) potential for firing a nerve action potential?
back: -55 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the approximate peak (overshoot) of the nerve action potential?
back: About +35 mV per the newer CoreBTR/BTR 3.0 source (matching the Na+ channel inactivation range); the older Cerebellum PDF graph shows a peak of approximately +30 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the Na+ channel in the resting (closed) state - gate status and function.
back: Activation gate is closed, inactivation gate is open; the channel is ready to open

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the Na+ channel in the activated (open) state - gate status and function.
back: Both activation and inactivation gates are open, allowing Na+ influx and depolarization

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the Na+ channel in the inactivated state - gate status and function.
back: Activation gate is open but inactivation gate is closed, so no Na+ entry occurs; this underlies the refractory period

subject: General Physiology
front: At what membrane potential is the Na+ channel in the resting state?
back: -90 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: Over what membrane potential range is the Na+ channel activated (open)?
back: -90 mV to +35 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: Over what membrane potential range is the Na+ channel inactivated?
back: +35 mV to -90 mV (inactivation is delayed)

subject: General Physiology
front: What defines the absolute refractory period and what is its duration?
back: No new action potential can be generated because Na+ channels are inactivated; it lasts about 2 milliseconds

subject: General Physiology
front: What defines the relative refractory period?
back: A stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed to generate a new action potential, due to the hyperpolarized state of the membrane

subject: General Physiology
front: What is accommodation?
back: When a prolonged sub-threshold stimulus is applied, the threshold itself increases, so no action potential is generated

subject: General Physiology
front: What is adaptation?
back: When a prolonged supra-threshold stimulus is applied, the firing rate decreases despite the continued stimulus

subject: General Physiology
front: How does hyperkalemia affect the resting membrane potential?
back: Extracellular K+ increases, reducing the outward K+ gradient, so less K+ leaves the cell; this makes the RMP more positive (less negative)

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens when a nerve action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal at the NMJ?
back: It depolarizes the terminal and opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels

subject: General Physiology
front: What triggers acetylcholine (ACh) release at the presynaptic terminal?
back: Ca2+ influx into the presynaptic terminal triggers ACh release via vesicle fusion

subject: General Physiology
front: Which receptor does ACh bind to on the muscle end plate?
back: Nicotinic ACh receptors

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens when ACh binds to nicotinic receptors on the end plate?
back: Ligand-gated Na+ channels open, causing Na+ influx and generating the end plate potential

subject: General Physiology
front: What does the end plate potential ultimately trigger?
back: Opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels that generate a muscle action potential leading to contraction

subject: General Physiology
front: Which part of the NMJ is affected in myasthenia gravis?
back: Post-synaptic nicotinic ACh receptors (antibodies against them)

subject: General Physiology
front: Which part of the NMJ is affected in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)?
back: Pre-synaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels

subject: General Physiology
front: What does Excitation-Contraction Coupling (ECC) link?
back: Muscle fiber electrical excitation to mechanical contraction

subject: General Physiology
front: List the sequential steps of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle.
back: 1) Depolarization of the sarcolemma 2) Action potential travels down T-tubules 3) Activates DHPR on T-tubules 4) DHPR (coupled to ryanodine receptors on the SR) opens SR Ca2+ channels 5) Cytosolic Ca2+ concentration increases 6) Ca2+ binds Troponin-C, exposing the actin binding site 7) Actin-myosin cross bridge forms and myosin pulls actin 8) ATP binds myosin, releasing the actin filament

subject: General Physiology
front: Why is cytosolic calcium described as crucial in muscle physiology?
back: Because cytosolic calcium is crucial for contraction

subject: General Physiology
front: Why is ATP described as crucial in muscle physiology?
back: Because ATP attachment to myosin is crucial for relaxation (release of the actin filament)

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens in the absence of ATP? Give a clinical example.
back: No relaxation occurs since myosin cannot release actin; the classic clinical example is rigor mortis

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens in the absence of calcium during excitation-contraction coupling?
back: No contraction occurs (calcium is required to bind troponin C and expose the actin-myosin binding site)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is cadaveric spasm and what is its forensic significance?
back: Instantaneous muscle stiffening that occurs at the moment of death without preceding relaxation; considered a sign of violent or ante-mortem death, such as drowning

subject: General Physiology
front: What pumps Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum to shut off the Ca2+ transient?
back: SERCA (SERCA1a), which reuptakes Ca2+ into the SR lumen

subject: General Physiology
front: What protein senses membrane depolarization in the T-tubule and opens the RyR channel on the SR?
back: DHPR (dihydropyridine receptor)

subject: General Physiology
front: What does calcium bind to on the actin filament to activate contraction?
back: Troponin C (part of the troponin complex)

subject: General Physiology
front: What normally covers the myosin-binding sites on actin at rest?
back: Tropomyosin

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe electromechanical coupling: location and receptor pairing.
back: Occurs in skeletal muscle; DHPR (CaV1) couples directly to RYR1; 100% of the Ca2+ used comes from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

subject: General Physiology
front: What gain-of-function mutation is associated with the DHPR-RYR1 (electromechanical) coupling?
back: Malignant hyperthermia

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe electrochemical coupling: location and receptor pairing.
back: Occurs in cardiac and smooth muscle; DHPR (CaV1.2/CaV2) couples to RYR2/RYR3

subject: General Physiology
front: What is CICR and what proportion of calcium does it involve?
back: Calcium-Induced Calcium Release - extracellular Ca2+ influx triggers further Ca2+ release from the SR; about 20% of the calcium used comes from outside the cell

subject: General Physiology
front: In smooth muscle, what does calcium bind to (in addition to troponin pathways in cardiac muscle)?
back: Calmodulin

subject: General Physiology
front: What does the calcium-calmodulin complex activate in smooth muscle, and what does it cause?
back: It activates MLCK (Myosin Light Chain Kinase), which phosphorylates MLC to cause contraction

subject: General Physiology
front: What causes relaxation in smooth muscle after MLC is phosphorylated?
back: Phosphatase dephosphorylates MLC, causing relaxation

subject: General Physiology
front: Summarize the core roles of calcium and ATP in muscle contraction.
back: Calcium drives contraction; ATP drives relaxation

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the three phases of a muscle twitch following an action potential?
back: Latent period, contraction period, and relaxation period

subject: General Physiology
front: What defines the contraction period of a muscle twitch?
back: The period from the end of the latent period to the point of maximum contraction

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens if a stimulus is given during the latent period?
back: No contraction occurs; the latent period corresponds to the absolute refractory period

subject: General Physiology
front: What is tetanus in the context of skeletal muscle physiology?
back: When a new action potential arrives within the contraction period of the previous twitch, causing summation of contractions

subject: General Physiology
front: What is tetanizing frequency and its formula?
back: The stimulus frequency required to produce tetanus; Tetanizing frequency = 1 / contraction period

subject: General Physiology
front: What results from a stimulus given during the period of relaxation?
back: Incomplete tetanus (partial summation)

subject: General Physiology
front: What results from a stimulus given during the period of contraction?
back: Complete tetanus (fully fused summation)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is Treppe (staircase phenomenon)?
back: When a muscle fiber is stimulated exactly at the end of the relaxation phase, resulting in increased tension and better muscle efficiency due to residual calcium

subject: General Physiology
front: What is Treppe considered the physiological basis of?
back: The basis of warm-up exercises

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens if a stimulus is given as soon as relaxation has finished (staircase pattern of stimuli)?
back: It produces the staircase/Treppe phenomenon with progressively increasing tension

subject: General Physiology
front: What type of reflex is the stretch reflex (spindle reflex) and what is its stimulus?
back: Monosynaptic reflex; stimulus is muscle stretch (change in length)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the afferent fiber type for the stretch reflex?
back: Ia fibers

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the response of the stretch reflex?
back: Agonist muscle contracts, antagonist muscle relaxes

subject: General Physiology
front: What type of reflex is the Golgi tendon reflex (inverse stretch reflex) and what is its stimulus?
back: Disynaptic reflex; stimulus is increased tension

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the afferent fiber type for the Golgi tendon reflex?
back: Ib fibers

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the response of the Golgi tendon reflex?
back: Agonist relaxes (autogenic inhibition)

subject: General Physiology
front: What type of reflex is the withdrawal reflex (flexor + crossed extensor) and what is its stimulus?
back: Polysynaptic reflex; stimulus is pain

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the afferent fiber type for the withdrawal reflex?
back: A-delta and C fibers

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the response pattern of the withdrawal reflex on the affected vs unaffected side?
back: Affected side: flexors contract, extensors relax. Unaffected side (crossed extensor reflex): extensors contract, flexors relax

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the function of the muscle spindle?
back: Acts as a stretch sensor inside the muscle

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the two types of intrafusal fibers in the muscle spindle?
back: Nuclear bag fibers and nuclear chain fibers

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the two subtypes of nuclear bag fibers and what do they detect?
back: Dynamic bag detects rate of stretch; static bag detects sustained stretch

subject: General Physiology
front: What does the nuclear chain fiber detect?
back: Only sustained stretch

subject: General Physiology
front: What does the Group Ia afferent (annulospiral ending) sense?
back: Both dynamic and static stretch

subject: General Physiology
front: What does the Group II afferent (flower-spray ending) sense?
back: Only static stretch

subject: General Physiology
front: In the Lloyd-Hunt classification of sensory nerves, what does class Ia correspond to?
back: Muscle spindle (annulospiral ending)

subject: General Physiology
front: In the Lloyd-Hunt classification of sensory nerves, what does class Ib correspond to?
back: Golgi tendon organ

subject: General Physiology
front: In the Lloyd-Hunt classification of sensory nerves, what does class II correspond to?
back: Muscle spindle (flower-spray ending)

subject: General Physiology
front: In the Lloyd-Hunt classification of sensory nerves, what does class III correspond to?
back: Pain and cold receptors

subject: General Physiology
front: In the Lloyd-Hunt classification of sensory nerves, what does class IV correspond to?
back: Pain and temperature receptors

subject: General Physiology
front: What is alpha-gamma coactivation?
back: Simultaneous activation of alpha and gamma motor neurons, so alpha motor neurons contract the extrafusal muscle while gamma motor neurons contract the intrafusal spindle fibers

subject: General Physiology
front: Why is gamma motor neuron activation necessary during muscle contraction?
back: Because when the muscle contracts the spindle becomes slack and cannot sense stretch; gamma activation keeps the spindle taut and maintains its sensitivity

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the length-tension relationship in skeletal muscle?
back: As sarcomere length increases from short, tension/force increases, reaches a maximum, then decreases

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the optimal sarcomere length for maximum tension development?
back: 2.0-2.2 micrometers (the B-C region of the length-tension curve)

subject: General Physiology
front: Which cardiovascular physiology law shares a concept similar to the skeletal muscle length-tension relationship?
back: Frank-Starling law

subject: General Physiology
front: What causes passive tension in a muscle?
back: Elastic connective tissue components within and around the muscle

subject: General Physiology
front: When does passive tension start to increase?
back: When the muscle is stretched beyond its resting length

subject: General Physiology
front: What does passive tension contribute to as sarcomere length increases beyond optimum?
back: It contributes to total tension, which may keep increasing even while active tension is declining

subject: General Physiology
front: What does the I-band of the sarcomere contain?
back: Only actin (thin filament)

subject: General Physiology
front: What does the A-band of the sarcomere contain?
back: Actin (thin filament), myosin (thick filament), the M-line, and the H-zone

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to the I-band during muscle contraction?
back: It shortens (mnemonic: "I contract")

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to the H-zone during muscle contraction?
back: It disappears (mnemonic: "H hides")

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to the A-band during muscle contraction?
back: It stays constant

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to the M-line during muscle contraction?
back: It becomes more prominent

subject: General Physiology
front: Which structural protein runs from the Z-line to the M-line, and what is notable about it?
back: Titin, which is the largest protein in the body

subject: General Physiology
front: Which structural protein anchors actin to the Z-line?
back: Alpha-actinin

subject: General Physiology
front: Which structural protein stabilizes actin filaments?
back: Nebulin

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the characteristics of Type-1 (slow, red) muscle fibers?
back: Increased blood vessels, increased myoglobin, increased mitochondria, and oxidative metabolism

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the characteristics of Type-2 (fast, white) muscle fibers?
back: Decreased blood vessels, decreased myoglobin, decreased mitochondria, and glycolytic metabolism

subject: General Physiology
front: What mnemonic describes Type-1 muscle fibers?
back: "1 slow red Ox" (Type 1 = slow, red, oxidative)

subject: General Physiology
front: How do ocular muscle, gastrocnemius, and soleus compare in speed of contraction (duration of depolarization)?
back: Ocular muscle is fastest (shortest duration/fast fiber type), gastrocnemius is intermediate, and soleus is slowest (longest duration, slow fiber type)

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: Where is the tight junction located and what is its function?
back: Located apicolaterally; it prevents paracellular movement, acting as a barrier

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: Which proteins compose the tight junction?
back: Claudin, occludin, and JAM (junctional adhesion molecule)

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What major physiological barrier is maintained by tight junctions?
back: The blood-brain barrier (BBB)

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What is ZOT and what toxin is it related to in the context of tight junctions?
back: ZOT (Zonula Occludens Toxin) is related to cholera toxin, which affects tight junction integrity in the gut

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What is the adherens junction also called, and which protein composes it?
back: Zonula adherens; composed of E-cadherin

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: Which malignancies are clinically associated with decreased E-cadherin?
back: Lobular breast carcinoma and diffuse gastric carcinoma

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What is the desmosome also called, and which protein composes it?
back: Macula adherens; composed of desmoglein

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What intracellular structures are desmosomes linked to?
back: Intermediate filaments (keratin)

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: Which antibody-mediated skin disease targets desmoglein at desmosomes?
back: Pemphigus (anti-desmoglein antibodies)

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What is the function of the gap junction and what is its structural unit?
back: Function is cell-to-cell communication (ions, electrical signals); structural unit is the connexon, made of 6 connexins

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: Where are gap junctions prominently located in the heart?
back: Intercalated discs of cardiac muscle

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: Which hereditary disease is associated with connexin gene defects?
back: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT), a hereditary sensorimotor neuropathy (HSMN)

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What is the function of the hemidesmosome?
back: Attaches the cell to the basement membrane

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: Which protein composes hemidesmosomes and what does it connect to?
back: Integrins, which connect to fibronectin/laminin and collagen in the extracellular matrix (ECM)

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: Which autoimmune blistering disease results from hemidesmosome/integrin dysfunction?
back: Bullous pemphigoid

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What are circumventricular organs?
back: Regions of the brain that lack a blood-brain barrier, allowing free exchange between blood and brain tissue

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What does the mnemonic "SOAP" stand for regarding BBB-absent areas?
back: Subfornical organ, Organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT), Area postrema, Pineal gland

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What is the function of the subfornical organ?
back: Circulating angiotensin II acts here to increase water intake (thirst)

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What is the function of the organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT)?
back: Acts as an osmoreceptor controlling vasopressin (ADH) secretion and thirst

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What is the function of the area postrema?
back: Acts as the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) that initiates vomiting in response to chemical changes in the plasma

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What is the function of the pineal body/gland?
back: Secretes melatonin hormone into the blood

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What does the posterior pituitary secrete, and why can it release hormones directly into blood?
back: Secretes hormones (ADH and oxytocin) into the blood; it lacks a BBB, allowing direct hormone release into systemic circulation

subject: General Physiology
front: What protein composes microfilaments and what are their main functions?
back: Actin; functions include muscle contraction and forming microvilli (involved in cytokinesis)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the main function of intermediate filaments?
back: To maintain the structural integrity of cells

subject: General Physiology
front: Match the intermediate filament immunohistochemistry markers to their cell type: Cytokeratin, Desmin, Vimentin, GFAP.
back: Cytokeratin - epithelial cells (carcinoma); Desmin - muscle; Vimentin - mesenchymal cells; GFAP - glial cells (per newer CoreBTR source; the older Cerebellum PDF lists GFAP as neuronal)

subject: General Physiology
front: Which intermediate filament type is found in Mallory-Denk bodies?
back: Keratin filaments

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the main functions of microtubules?
back: Movement and cell division - including cilia, flagella, mitotic spindle, centrioles, and axoplasmic transport in neurons

subject: General Physiology
front: What mnemonic describes microtubule function?
back: "Moves through tube"

subject: General Physiology
front: What is axoplasmic transport and what are its two directions?
back: Movement of material along microtubules within neurons; retrograde (toward the cell body) and antegrade/anterograde (toward the axon terminal)

subject: General Physiology
front: Which motor protein mediates retrograde axoplasmic transport, and in which direction does it move?
back: Dynein; moves from the +ve end (axon terminal) toward the -ve end (cell body)

subject: General Physiology
front: Which motor protein mediates antegrade (anterograde) axoplasmic transport, and in which direction does it move?
back: Kinesin; moves from the -ve end (cell body) toward the +ve end (axon terminal)

subject: General Physiology
front: Which agents/pathogens use retrograde axoplasmic transport to reach the CNS?
back: Polio virus, tetanus toxin, rabies virus, and HSV (the older Cerebellum PDF also lists botulinum toxin in this group)

subject: General Physiology
front: Which process is associated with antegrade axoplasmic transport?
back: Reactivation of HSV/VZV, traveling from the ganglion (cell body) toward the periphery

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the mnemonic for drugs that act on the mitotic spindle (microtubules), and which drugs does it include?
back: "Microtubules Get Contracted Very Tightly" - Mebendazole, Griseofulvin, Colchicine, Vinca alkaloids, and Taxanes

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the microtubule arrangement of a motile cilium?
back: 9+2 arrangement - 9 peripheral doublets plus 2 central singlets

subject: General Physiology
front: How does a primary cilium's microtubule arrangement differ from a motile cilium?
back: A primary cilium has a 9+0 arrangement, lacking the central pair of microtubules found in motile cilia

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the microtubule arrangement of the basal body?
back: 9 triplets (no central pair)

subject: General Physiology
front: What structural defect underlies Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome)?
back: A defect in the dynein arm of cilia

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the clinical tetrad of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome)?
back: Situs inversus (with dextrocardia), bronchiectasis, sinusitis, and infertility

subject: General Physiology
front: What defines isotonic (dynamic) exercise, and what are examples?
back: Muscle length changes with contraction and relaxation; examples include running and cycling

subject: General Physiology
front: What defines isometric (static) exercise, and what are examples?
back: Muscle length remains constant during sustained contraction; examples include handgrip and weight holding

subject: General Physiology
front: How does isotonic exercise affect TPR, and why?
back: TPR decreases (vasodilation) because alternating muscle contraction and relaxation opens the vessels

subject: General Physiology
front: How does isotonic exercise affect stroke volume and MAP?
back: Stroke volume increases (raising cardiac output), so MAP remains constant or increases despite the fall in TPR

subject: General Physiology
front: How does isometric exercise affect blood vessels and TPR?
back: Sustained contraction compresses blood vessels, increasing TPR (a vasoconstriction-like effect)

subject: General Physiology
front: How does isometric exercise affect DBP and MAP?
back: Both DBP and MAP increase due to the rise in TPR

subject: General Physiology
front: Compare CO, HR, SV, SBP, TPR, DBP, and MAP in isotonic vs isometric exercise.
back: Isotonic: CO up, HR up, SV up, SBP up, TPR down, DBP down, MAP constant/down. Isometric: CO up, HR up, SV normal (unchanged), SBP up, DBP up, TPR up, MAP up

subject: General Physiology
front: By how much does skeletal muscle blood flow increase during exercise compared to rest?
back: Up to 20 times (20x) the resting value

subject: General Physiology
front: What is resting vs exercising skeletal muscle blood flow (per 100 g tissue per minute)?
back: Rest: 2-4 mL/100g/min (about 16% of cardiac output); Exercise: 50-80 mL/100g/min

subject: General Physiology
front: Rank organ blood flow changes during exercise from greatest increase to decrease.
back: Muscular > Coronary > Cerebral > Renal/Splanchnic (renal and splanchnic flow decreases during exercise)

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to coronary blood flow during exercise?
back: It increases

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to cerebral blood flow during exercise?
back: It remains constant

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to renal and splanchnic blood flow during exercise?
back: Both decrease

subject: General Physiology
front: What is reactive hyperemia in the context of isotonic exercise blood flow?
back: A transient increase in blood flow above baseline that occurs after muscle compressions/contractions end

subject: General Physiology
front: List the energy sources used during exercise, in order of use.
back: Stored ATP (immediate), creatine phosphate, anaerobic glycolysis (anaerobic metabolism), and aerobic metabolism

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to minute ventilation during exercise?
back: It increases

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to the V/Q ratio during exercise?
back: It improves (better ventilation-perfusion matching, similar to lung zone 2-3)

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve during exercise, and why does this matter?
back: It shifts to the right, allowing better delivery of oxygen to tissues

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to PaO2 during exercise?
back: It remains approximately normal/constant

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to PvO2 during exercise, and why?
back: It decreases due to increased oxygen uptake by the tissues

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to PaCO2 during exercise, and why?
back: It decreases due to hyperventilation

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to pH during exercise, and why?
back: It decreases, especially in severe exercise, due to lactic acidosis

subject: General Physiology
front: What does the Nernst equation calculate?
back: The equilibrium potential of an ion - the potential at which electrical force balances the chemical (concentration) gradient

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the formula for the Nernst equation?
back: V(eq) = (RT/zF) x ln([X]out/[X]in), approximately equal to +/-61 x log([X]out/[X]in)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the equilibrium potential of Na+?
back: +60 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the equilibrium potential of Ca2+?

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the equilibrium potential of Cl-?
back: -70 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the equilibrium potential of K+?
back: -90 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: Which ion has the most positive equilibrium potential, and which has the most negative?
back: Calcium (Ca2+) is most positive; potassium (K+) is most negative

subject: General Physiology
front: What does the Goldman equation calculate, and how does it differ from the Nernst equation?
back: It calculates the resting membrane potential (RMP), taking into account multiple ions and their relative membrane permeabilities (unlike Nernst, which is for a single ion)

subject: General Physiology
front: Why is RMP approximately equal to the K+ equilibrium potential?
back: Because the membrane has open leaky K+ channels, making it mainly permeable to K+ at rest

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the RMP of neurons?
back: -70 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the RMP of skeletal muscle?
back: -90 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the RMP of cardiac myocytes?
back: -90 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the RMP of pacemaker cells?
back: -60 mV

subject: General Physiology
front: Which cells are considered pacemaker cells, and why can they spontaneously depolarize?
back: SA node cells, interstitial cells of Cajal, and the pre-Botzinger complex; their comparatively less negative RMP allows spontaneous depolarization

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the Gibbs-Donnan effect?
back: Alteration of the distribution of permeable ions across a membrane due to the presence of large impermeable charged molecules (proteins) inside the cell

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the effects of the Gibbs-Donnan effect on intracellular ion distribution?
back: Increased intracellular cations (K+), decreased intracellular anions (Cl-), and creation of an osmotic gradient

subject: General Physiology
front: What is Poiseuille's Law and its formula for flow through a tube?
back: Q = (pi x P x r^4) / (8 x eta x l), where Q is flow rate, P is pressure, r is radius, eta is fluid viscosity, and l is length of the tube

subject: General Physiology
front: How does flow relate to radius and length according to Poiseuille's Law?
back: Flow is proportional to radius to the 4th power (r^4) and inversely proportional to length (1/length); a small change in radius causes a huge change in flow

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the percentage composition of the cell membrane according to the Singer-Nicolson Fluid Mosaic Model?
back: Protein 55%, Phospholipid 25%, Cholesterol 13%, Carbohydrate 3%

subject: General Physiology
front: What percentage of the inner mitochondrial membrane is protein?
back: 90% protein

subject: General Physiology
front: How do the hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions of the phospholipid bilayer orient?
back: The outer layer is hydrophilic (facing the aqueous environment); the inner layer is hydrophobic (tails facing each other)

subject: General Physiology
front: What role does cholesterol play in the cell membrane?
back: It maintains membrane fluidity and stability

subject: General Physiology
front: Are triglycerides part of the cell membrane?
back: No, triglycerides (TG) are NOT part of the cell membrane

subject: General Physiology
front: What does the Singer-Nicolson Fluid Mosaic Model describe?
back: The cell membrane as a dynamic, fluid lipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it like a mosaic

subject: General Physiology
front: Define rheobase.
back: The minimum current/voltage strength required to excite a tissue, irrespective of stimulus duration

subject: General Physiology
front: Define chronaxie.
back: The minimum duration of stimulus required to excite a tissue when using a current of twice the rheobase strength

subject: General Physiology
front: Define utilization time.
back: The time required to excite a tissue when the stimulus strength is exactly at rheobase

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the mechanism of coughing and what it clears.
back: Deep inspiration followed by forced expiration against a closed glottis, then sudden opening of the glottis; clears the lower respiratory tract

subject: General Physiology
front: Describe the mechanism of sneezing and what it clears.
back: Forced expiration through an open glottis; clears the nasal passages and upper respiratory tract

subject: General Physiology
front: What concept did Walter Cannon introduce?
back: The concept of homeostasis - maintenance of internal stability

subject: General Physiology
front: What clinical marker is linked to Walter Cannon's homeostasis concept?
back: Urine output, which reflects perfusion and organ function

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the two types of feedback regulatory mechanisms in the body?
back: Negative feedback and positive feedback

subject: General Physiology
front: Which type of feedback is the most common in physiological systems?
back: Negative feedback

subject: General Physiology
front: Give three examples of negative feedback mechanisms.
back: Baroreceptor reflex, chemoreceptor reflex, and core body temperature regulation

subject: General Physiology
front: List six examples of positive feedback mechanisms in the body.
back: Parturition (Ferguson reflex), milk ejection (oxytocin), blood clotting cascade, calcium-induced calcium release (CICR), LH surge (ovulation), and the Hodgkin cycle (Na+ channel opening during an action potential)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is feed-forward (anticipatory) regulation?
back: A regulatory mechanism in which the body makes adjustments in anticipation of an event, before it actually occurs

subject: General Physiology
front: Give four examples of feed-forward mechanisms.
back: Salivation on thinking about food, the cephalic phase of gastric acid secretion, anticipatory tachycardia, and pre-emptive temperature regulation adjustments

subject: General Physiology
front: What is anticipatory tachycardia?
back: An increase in heart rate that occurs in anticipation of an activity or event, before it actually begins

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the formula for the gain of a control system?
back: Gain = Correction / Error

subject: General Physiology
front: In a baroreceptor example, normal MAP is 100 mmHg. Without the baroreceptor reflex, MAP rises to 175 mmHg; with the reflex, it is corrected to 125 mmHg. What is the gain?
back: Correction = 175-125 = 50 mmHg; Error = 125-100 = 25 mmHg; Gain = 50/25 = 2

subject: General Physiology
front: Which three taste modalities use GPCR-type receptors, and what is the mnemonic?
back: Sweet, Umami, and Bitter; mnemonic is "SUB"

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the example receptor for sweet, umami, and bitter taste (GPCR-mediated)?
back: TAS1R2 + TAS1R3

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the receptor type for sour taste, and what are example receptor proteins?
back: Ion channel (H+-sensing); example receptors are PKD2L1 and TRPV1

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the receptor type for salty taste, and what is the example receptor protein?
back: Ion channel (Na+-sensing); example receptor is ENaC

subject: General Physiology
front: What class of substances typically transmits bitter taste?
back: Alkaloids (often toxic substances)

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to FiO2 and atmospheric pressure at high altitude?
back: FiO2 (fraction of inspired O2) remains essentially normal, but atmospheric (barometric) pressure decreases

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to PaO2 at high altitude?
back: It decreases

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to ventilation at high altitude, and why?
back: Ventilation increases due to the hypoxic drive, causing CO2 washout

subject: General Physiology
front: What acid-base disturbance occurs at high altitude?
back: Respiratory alkalosis, due to hyperventilation and CO2 washout

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to 2,3-BPG at high altitude and what effect does this have on oxygen delivery?
back: 2,3-BPG increases, causing a rightward shift of the oxygen-dissociation curve, which reduces hemoglobin's O2 affinity and aids O2 unloading to tissues

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) at high altitude?
back: It increases, due to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the pharmacological treatment for acute mountain sickness?
back: Acetazolamide

subject: General Physiology
front: What are HAPE and HACE, and how are they managed?
back: High Altitude Pulmonary Edema and High Altitude Cerebral Edema; managed by rapid descent and administration of 100% oxygen

subject: General Physiology
front: What is barotrauma in diving, and what are its manifestations?
back: Injury caused by pressure changes during diving; can cause pneumothorax (PTx) or tympanic membrane (TM) rupture

subject: General Physiology
front: What is Caisson disease (decompression sickness), and how is it prevented?
back: Nitrogen bubble formation in tissues/joints (causing arthritis-like symptoms) upon rapid ascent from depth; prevented and managed by slow, gradual ascent

subject: General Physiology
front: What is the Carrageenan theory used for?
back: It is an experimental model used to study and induce inflammation

subject: General Physiology
front: Where is the Windkessel effect seen, and where is it absent?
back: Seen in the aorta and large elastic arteries; absent in peripheral muscular arteries

subject: General Physiology
front: What percentage of total body weight do ICF and ECF each represent?
back: ICF is about 40% of body weight and ECF is about 20% of body weight (since TBW = 60% of body weight, split 2/3 : 1/3)

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF calcium (Ca2+) concentrations?
back: ECF: about 2.4 mEq/L; ICF: about 0.0001 mEq/L

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF magnesium (Mg2+) concentrations?
back: ECF: about 1.2 mEq/L; ICF: about 58 mEq/L

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF chloride (Cl-) concentrations?
back: ECF: about 103 mEq/L; ICF: about 4 mEq/L

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF bicarbonate (HCO3-) concentrations?
back: ECF: about 28 mEq/L; ICF: about 10 mEq/L

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF phosphate concentrations?
back: ECF: about 4 mEq/L; ICF: about 75 mEq/L

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF sulfate (SO4) concentrations?
back: ECF: about 1 mEq/L; ICF: about 2 mEq/L

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF glucose concentrations?
back: ECF: about 90 mg/dL; ICF: about 0-20 mg/dL

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF amino acid concentrations?
back: ECF: about 30 mg/dL; ICF: about 200 mg/dL

subject: General Physiology
front: How do ECF and ICF compare for cholesterol, phospholipid, and neutral fat content?
back: ECF is low (about 0.5-2 g/dL); ICF is much higher (up to about 95 g/dL)

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF PO2 values?
back: ECF: about 35 mmHg; ICF: about 20 mmHg

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF PCO2 values?
back: ECF: about 46 mmHg; ICF: about 50 mmHg

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the approximate ECF vs ICF pH values (numeric)?
back: ECF: about 7.4; ICF: about 7.0

subject: General Physiology
front: What stimuli drive the increase in ventilation during exercise?
back: Proprioceptor input from muscles/joints, increased K+, increased temperature, and decreased pH act via chemoreceptors to raise ventilation

subject: General Physiology
front: What happens to PvCO2 (venous CO2) during exercise?
back: It increases, since exercising tissues produce more CO2

subject: General Physiology
front: How does muscle blood flow behave during rhythmic isotonic contractions (moment-to-moment), as distinct from the overall mean increase?
back: Blood flow rises and falls with each individual contraction (falling during compression, rising during relaxation), while the mean flow over time is increased

subject: General Physiology
front: According to the older Cerebellum PDF, how does MAP change specifically during severe isotonic exercise?
back: MAP tends to rise with mild-to-moderate isotonic exercise (driven by increased SV/CO) but then falls in severe isotonic exercise as vasodilation (falling TPR) starts to dominate

subject: General Physiology
front: How does the rise in MAP with increasing exercise intensity compare between isometric and isotonic exercise?
back: Isometric exercise produces a steeper, more sustained rise in MAP than isotonic exercise as intensity increases from rest to severe

subject: General Physiology
front: At approximately what time point during exercise does each energy source peak in its contribution?
back: Stored ATP peaks almost immediately (~2 seconds), creatine phosphate peaks around 10 seconds, anaerobic glycolysis peaks around 1 minute, and aerobic metabolism becomes dominant by about 2 hours for sustained performance

subject: General Physiology
front: In the Nernst equation V = (RT/zF) ln([X]out/[X]in), what do R, T, z, and F represent?
back: R = universal gas constant, T = temperature, z = valency (charge) of the ion, F = Faraday's constant

subject: General Physiology
front: What is endocrine signaling?
back: A hormone is released into the bloodstream to act on distant target cells

subject: General Physiology
front: What is autocrine signaling? Give an example.
back: A cell signals to itself; example - PAF (platelet activating factor)

subject: General Physiology
front: What is paracrine signaling? Give an example.
back: A cell signals to nearby neighboring cells; example - somatostatin

subject: General Physiology
front: What is juxtacrine signaling? Give an example.
back: Signaling that requires direct cell-to-cell contact; example - TGF-alpha

subject: General Physiology
front: What theory explains how TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) relieves pain, and which spinal structure is involved?
back: The Gate Control Theory of pain; it acts via the substantia gelatinosa in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord

subject: General Physiology
front: Which ion's equilibrium potential is closest to the neuronal RMP, and which is closest to the RMP of muscle (skeletal/cardiac)?
back: Cl- equilibrium potential (-70 mV) is closest to neuronal RMP (-70 mV); K+ equilibrium potential (-90 mV) is closest to skeletal/cardiac muscle RMP (-90 mV)

subject: General Physiology
front: Why might the gain of a negative feedback system sometimes be expressed as a negative number?
back: Because the correction opposes the direction of the initial deviation; the older Cerebellum PDF computes the baroreceptor example as Correction = -50, Error = 25, Gain = -50/25 = -2 (signed), whereas the newer BTR 3.0 source uses absolute magnitudes to get Gain = +2

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: Besides being apicolateral in general, where specifically are tight junctions highlighted in the notes?
back: At the brush border on the apical side of enterocytes, and in the brush border of the PCT/DCT (proximal and distal convoluted tubules) of the kidney

subject: General Physiology
deck: Part 6 - Epithelial Cell Junctions & Circumventricular Organs
front: What functional property do gap junctions create among connected cells?
back: An electrical syncytium, allowing connected cells to function as a single electrical unit

subject: General Physiology
front: What are the key structural components of a ciliary microtubule doublet?
back: Two microtubules (labeled A and B), dynein arms (which drive movement), and nexin links (which connect adjacent doublets)
